abstract.text: Aspects of scientific method are discussed: In particular, its representation as a motivated iteration in which, in succession, practice confronts theory, and theory, practice. Rapid progress requires sufficient flexibility to profit from such confrontations, and the ability to devise parsimonious but effective models, to worry selectively about model inadequacies and to employ mathematics skillfully but appropriately. The development of statistical methods at Rothamsted Experimental Station by Sir Ronald Fisher is used to illustrate these themes.

predecessors.cited_work: classical accounts of scientific method and Fisher's own practical work
predecessors.reference_key: Aristotle; Galen; Grosstete; William of Occam; Bacon
predecessors.why: the text explicitly traces the heritage of thought about scientific method to these writers and builds its argument upon Fisher's practice.

replications.cited_work: Fisher's own model of theory--practice iteration
replications.why: the paper repeatedly reads Fisher's work as concrete iterations between practical problems and theoretical models.

targets.why: the paper argues that statistical work that loses contact with either theory or practice stagnates.

thesis.text: Scientific and statistical progress comes from a motivated feedback iteration between theory and practice, requiring flexibility, parsimonious models, selective worry about model inadequacies, and appropriately used mathematics; Fisher's Rothamsted work illustrates this process.

citations.context: In reality this main iteration is accompanied by many simultaneous subiterations (see, e.g., [1, 2]).
Sir John Russell, then Director of Rothamsted, later recalled [17, p. 326]
This resulted in Fisher's pioneering work on nonlinear design in 1922 mentioned by Cochran [4].
His first example is introduced as follows [12, p. 25]: "Figure 1 represents the growth of a baby weighed to the nearest ounce at equal intervals from birth."

The extraordinary extent to which Fisher's actual every day experience was grist to the mill of his inductive mind is further illustrated in the famous opening lines of Chapter II of Fisher's book The Design of Experiments [11, p. 11]: "A lady declares that by tasting a cup of tea... she can discriminate whether the milk or the tea infusion was first added to the cup."
The authors note [14, p. 180] that, "the limiting distribution must be such that the extreme member of a sample of n from such a distribution has itself a similar distribution."

In "Studies in Crop Variation I" [7], Fisher begins by presenting a workmanlike discussion, which lasts for twelve pages, of the responses to the thirteen different manures revealed by his analysis of the Broadbalk data.

In "Studies in Crop Variation II," jointly authored with his assistant, Miss W.A. MacKenzie, and subtitled "The Manurial Response of Different Potato Varieties," [13] he tried his hand at analyzing some experimental data from Rothamsted.
Fisher says [7, p. 123] "it is a weakness of the polynomial form that the extreme terms should be so much affected."
He speculates [7, p. 129], "Of all the organic factors which influence the yield of wheat it is probable that weeds alone change sufficiently slowly to explain the changes at Broadbalk."
But he says [7, p. 131] "it may be remembered that the Education Acts of 1876 and 1880 made attendance at school compulsory."
In the third paper of the series [8], he used the Broadbalk data to demonstrate the influence of rainfall on the wheat yield.

After the algebraic identity between the total suin of squares and the within and between treatments suni of squares has been written down, the statement is made [13, p. 315] "If all the plots were undifferentiated, as if the numbers had been mixed up and written down in random order, the average value of each of the two parts is proportional to the number of degrees of freedom in the variation of which it is compared."
Indeed, much can still be learnt from his discussion about economical processes of calculation and appropriate checks [8, p. 111-3].
form of the appropriate correction came quickly in the first edition of Statistical Methods in 1925 (see [12, p. 238]).

The authors say [13, p. 316], "the above test is only given as an illustration of the method; the summation formula for combining the effects of variety and manurial treatment is evidently quite unsuitable for the purpose. No one would expect to obtain from a low yielding variety the same actual increase in yield which a high yielding variety would give... a far more natural assumption is that the yield should be the product of two factors one depending on the variety and one on the manure."

With the possibility of transformation so much a part of Fisher's everyday thought, we might expect him now to proceed along that route but in fact he derives the appropriate nonlinear analysis, devising methods which have only recently been rediscovered [18].
When Fisher's friend Gosset saw the paper, he wrote to Fisher [15, Letter No. 29], "The experiment seems to me to be quite badly planned, you should give them a hand in that....."
Fisher later notes Gosset's "suggesting that I should start designing experiments" [15, summary of Letter No. 29].
But between 1924 and 1929, as described in "Studies in Crop Variation IV and VI" [5, 6], there is a rapid development of ideas which were quickly put into practice.

In spite of all this in 1926 the Director of Rothamsted, Sir John Russell, wrote a paper [16] in the Journal of the Ministry of Agriculture about agricultural experimentation which almost totally ignored the ideas of his proteg6.
However, in the next issue [9] in a paper notable for its brevity and clarity, Fisher outlined his philosophy on the subject, setting his boss to rights and anyone else who would listen.
I have cited already the development of distribution-free tests which, he felt, misused ideas initiated in Chapter III of his book Design of Experiments [11, p. 48].
As long ago as 1950, Fisher, delivering the Eddington Memorial Lecture at Cambridge, said [10, p. 22]

To quote Fisher once more, in 1952, in a letter concerning a proposed Statistics Center to be set up in Scotland he said: "I have no hesitation in advising that such a centre as you have under discussion should plan to integrate teaching closely with project work in which practical experience can be gained by those who are capable of learning from it; in contradistinction to the ruinous process of segregating the keener minds into a completely sterile atmosphere" [3].

sections.summary: Science advances through motivated feedback between theory and practice; flexibility, parsimony, selective worry, and appropriate mathematics are its disciplines. Fisher's move to Rothamsted opens the illustrative case.
sections.title: The Iterative Method of Science

source_span.end_text: 3.6 From Dung to Orthogonal Polynomials and Residual Analysis

sections.summary: Fisher's practical curiosity---baby weights, the tea-tasting lady, bacterial counts, cotton strength---turns ordinary experience into statistical problems and initiates theory--practice iterations.
sections.title: Everyday Experience as Fisher's Raw Material

source_span.end_text: 3.8 From Rainfall and Wheat Yield to Distributed Lags
source_span.start_text: 3.6 From Dung to Orthogonal Polynomials and Residual Analysis

sections.summary: Fisher's Broadbalk analyses show parsimonious modeling, residual diagnostics, orthogonal polynomials, and distributed-lag rainfall models as concrete instances of data analysis feeding theory.
sections.title: Parsimonious Models, Residuals, and Distributed Lags

source_span.start_text: 3.9 From Fertilizer and Potatoes to the Analysis of Variance

sections.summary: The potato experiment leads to the analysis of variance and nonlinear analysis; randomization grounds validity; Fisher then develops and sells blocking, factorial, confounding, and a new statistician role.
sections.title: Analysis of Variance, Randomization, and Design

sections.summary: When feedback is absent, statistics falls into cookbookery or mathematistry; the remedy is hard facts, real problems, and training statisticians as scientists. Fisher's example concludes.
sections.title: Open-Loop Perils, Mathematistry, and Training

thesis.text: Scientific and statistical progress comes from a motivated feedback iteration between theory and practice, requiring flexibility, parsimonious models, selective worry about model inadequacies, and appropriately used mathematics; Fisher's Rothamsted work illustrates this process.

His first example is introduced as follows [12, p. 25]: "Figure 1 represents the growth of a baby weighed to the nearest ounce at equal intervals from birth."

The extraordinary extent to which Fisher's actual every day experience was grist to the mill of his inductive mind is further illustrated in the famous opening lines of Chapter II of Fisher's book The Design of Experiments [11, p. 11]: "A lady declares that by tasting a cup of tea... she can discriminate whether the milk or the tea infusion was first added to the cup."

In "Studies in Crop Variation II," jointly authored with his assistant, Miss W.A. MacKenzie, and subtitled "The Manurial Response of Different Potato Varieties," [13] he tried his hand at analyzing some experimental data from Rothamsted.

After the algebraic identity between the total suin of squares and the within and between treatments suni of squares has been written down, the statement is made [13, p. 315] "If all the plots were undifferentiated, as if the numbers had been mixed up and written down in random order, the average value of each of the two parts is proportional to the number of degrees of freedom in the variation of which it is compared."
Indeed, much can still be learnt from his discussion about economical processes of calculation and appropriate checks [8, p. 111-3].

The authors say [13, p. 316], "the above test is only given as an illustration of the method; the summation formula for combining the effects of variety and manurial treatment is evidently quite unsuitable for the purpose. No one would expect to obtain from a low yielding variety the same actual increase in yield which a high yielding variety would give... a far more natural assumption is that the yield should be the product of two factors one depending on the variety and one on the manure."

With the possibility of transformation so much a part of Fisher's everyday thought, we might expect him now to proceed along that route but in fact he derives the appropriate nonlinear analysis, devising methods which have only recently been rediscovered [18].
When Fisher's friend Gosset saw the paper, he wrote to Fisher [15, Letter No. 29], "The experiment seems to me to be quite badly planned, you should give them a hand in that....."
Fisher later notes Gosset's "suggesting that I should start designing experiments" [15, summary of Letter No. 29].
But between 1924 and 1929, as described in "Studies in Crop Variation IV and VI" [5, 6], there is a rapid development of ideas which were quickly put into practice.

In spite of all this in 1926 the Director of Rothamsted, Sir John Russell, wrote a paper [16] in the Journal of the Ministry of Agriculture about agricultural experimentation which almost totally ignored the ideas of his proteg6.
However, in the next issue [9] in a paper notable for its brevity and clarity, Fisher outlined his philosophy on the subject, setting his boss to rights and anyone else who would listen.
